topic: What is a systematic investment plan (SIP) and how does it work
outline: How a SIP works step by step
Rupee cost averaging: what it does and does not do
Costs, lock-ins and rules to check
What happens if an instalment fails
facts: A SIP is a method of investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund scheme at regular intervals, such as monthly. It is not a separate product.
The investor chooses the scheme, the amount, the date and the frequency, and sets up an auto-debit instruction (mandate) with their bank.
On each date the amount buys units at that day's net asset value (NAV), so more units are allotted when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high.
This averaging of purchase cost is called rupee cost averaging. It reduces dependence on picking a single entry point but does not protect against losses or guarantee returns.
Mutual fund returns are not guaranteed and the NAV can fall as well as rise.
Minimum SIP amounts and available frequencies differ by fund house and scheme, so check the scheme documents.
Most open-ended funds have no lock-in, but ELSS tax-saving funds carry a 3-year lock-in that applies separately to each SIP instalment.
Some schemes charge an exit load if units are redeemed within a period set by the scheme, so check the scheme documents.
Gains are taxed under the rules in force at the time of redemption, and these rules change, so check the current rules.
KYC verification is required before investing in mutual funds.
Investors can usually pause or stop a SIP, subject to the fund house's rules and notice periods.
The right scheme depends on the investor's time horizon and risk tolerance.
A lump sum investment buys units at a single NAV on one date, while a SIP spreads purchases across several dates.
If a SIP instalment cannot be debited because the bank account has insufficient balance, that instalment is not invested, and the bank may charge a fee for the failed debit.
Fund houses may cancel a SIP after repeated failed debits, according to their own rules.
If a SIP date falls on a holiday, the instalment is typically processed on the next business day.
Direct plans and regular plans of the same scheme differ in expenses, because regular plans include a distributor commission.
Mutual funds in India are regulated by SEBI, and AMFI publishes NAVs and investor information.
The scheme information document and the fact sheet list the investment objective, expenses, exit load and risk level of a scheme.

topic: Term insurance versus endowment plans: the basic difference
outline: Premiums and what they depend on
facts: A pure term plan pays the sum assured to the nominee if the policyholder dies during the policy term; it pays nothing if the policyholder survives the term.
An endowment plan combines life cover with savings: it pays a death benefit during the term and a maturity benefit if the policyholder survives.
Because part of an endowment premium goes to the savings component, premiums are generally higher than for a pure term plan with the same life cover.
Some term plans offer a return of premium option, which raises the premium.
In traditional endowment plans, only part of the maturity amount may be guaranteed; bonuses, where offered, are not guaranteed.
Compare the sum assured, policy term, premium payment term, exclusions, and the insurer's claim settlement record.
Exclusions and conditions differ by insurer and are listed in the policy document.
Health and lifestyle details must be disclosed accurately at purchase, since non-disclosure can lead to a claim being rejected.
Insurers in India are regulated by the IRDAI.
Insurance needs differ by person; this article is educational and not a recommendation of any plan.
This article compares two kinds of life insurance plan: term plans and endowment plans.
A term plan premium depends on factors such as the policyholder age, the sum assured, the policy term and the insurer assessment of health and lifestyle.
The policy term and the premium payment term can differ in some plans, so check both in the policy document.
Surrendering an endowment plan before maturity can return less than the premiums paid, depending on the surrender terms in the policy.
The claim settlement ratio is a published figure showing the share of claims an insurer settled in a year, and it does not predict how any individual claim will be treated.
The policyholder names a nominee to receive the benefit, and nominee details can be updated as circumstances change.
Riders such as accidental death or critical illness cover can be added to some plans for an additional premium, and the available riders differ by insurer and plan.
Tax treatment of premiums and benefits depends on the rules in force at the time, which change, so check the current rules.
A free-look period lets a policyholder review a new policy and return it if the terms are not acceptable, subject to the insurer rules.

What Is NAV in a Mutual Fund and How Is It Calculated?
topic: What is NAV in a mutual fund and how is it calculated
outline: Which NAV applies to your purchase
What NAV does and does not tell you
facts: NAV stands for Net Asset Value and is the per-unit value of a mutual fund scheme.
NAV is calculated as the market value of the scheme's assets minus its liabilities, divided by the number of units outstanding.
Assets are valued at the closing market prices of the securities the scheme holds, so NAV changes from day to day as those prices change.
Unlike a share price, which moves during market hours, a scheme's NAV is declared at the end of each trading day after markets close.
Fund houses publish NAVs every business day on their own websites and on AMFI's website.
For most schemes, units are allotted at the prospective NAV, which is the NAV declared at the end of the day based on closing prices. Liquid and overnight funds follow different rules.
Which day NAV applies depends on the cut-off time and on when the money is available. An application received after the cut-off time gets the NAV of the next business day.
Cut-off times are set out in the scheme documents.
The number of units allotted is the amount invested divided by the NAV. For example, an investment of ₹10,000 at a NAV of ₹20 buys 500 units.
A fund with a NAV of ₹10 and a fund with a NAV of ₹50 that each rise by 10% give the same percentage gain, so a lower NAV does not mean a fund is cheaper.
NAV does not show how good a fund is. What matters is how the NAV changes over time and what the fund costs.
Scheme expenses are deducted from the scheme's assets, so they are reflected in the daily NAV and not billed separately.
Direct and regular plans of the same scheme have separate NAVs.
Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks, so read all scheme-related documents carefully.

For example, a scheme with assets worth ₹110 crore, liabilities of ₹10 crore and 10 crore units outstanding has a NAV of ₹10, because ₹110 crore minus ₹10 crore is ₹100 crore, and ₹100 crore divided by 10 crore units is ₹10.
If the NAV later rises from ₹20 to ₹22, 500 units that were worth ₹10,000 are then worth ₹11,000.
The NAV can also fall, in which case the same units are worth less than the amount invested.
The NAV is quoted per unit, so it does not show the size of a scheme. Assets under management show that.
On redemption, the amount paid is the number of units multiplied by the applicable NAV, less any exit load.

title: Direct vs Regular Mutual Fund Plans: What the Difference Means
topic: Direct versus regular mutual fund plans: what the difference means
outline: Separate NAVs and what that means
How to tell which plan you hold
facts: Every mutual fund scheme can be held through a direct plan or a regular plan.
In a direct plan the investor invests without routing the investment through a distributor or agent. In a regular plan the investment is made with the help of a distributor or agent.
A direct plan and a regular plan belong to the same scheme, share the same portfolio and are managed by the same fund manager.
The two plans have different expense ratios, because a direct plan has no distribution cost or commission.
SEBI has noted that distribution expenses and commission cannot be charged to investors of a direct plan, so the direct plan has a lower expense ratio and the two plans show different returns.
Because the expense ratios differ, each plan has its own NAV, and the direct plan has the higher NAV.
AMFI notes that the difference between the two NAVs tends to be small.
Over time the lower cost of a direct plan can add to returns, and this difference keeps compounding.
AMFI describes direct plans as meant for investors who prefer to invest without a distributor's help, and regular plans as the route for investors who want guidance and assistance.
Banks commonly act as distributors, so investing through a bank is generally a regular plan and not a direct plan.
Regular plan investments are made under the distributor's AMFI registration number, known as an ARN.
Schemes show direct or regular in the plan name, and SEBI requires expenses and returns to be disclosed separately for direct and regular plans.
Moving from a regular plan to a direct plan can involve an exit load and tax on gains, so check the scheme documents and the current tax rules first.
The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 changed how expense limits are defined from 1 April 2026, so check the current expense ratio in the scheme documents.

title: What Is an Expense Ratio in Mutual Funds and How Does It Work?
topic: What is an expense ratio in mutual funds and how does it work
outline: How the cost reaches you through NAV
Where to find a scheme expense ratio
facts: An expense ratio is the yearly cost of running a mutual fund scheme, charged to the scheme's assets and shown as a percentage.
Investors do not get a separate bill. The expenses are reflected in the scheme's daily NAV.
The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced the 1996 regulations, and the revised expense framework applies from 1 April 2026.
Under the new framework the Total Expense Ratio (TER) is the sum of the Base Expense Ratio (BER), brokerage, regulatory levies and statutory levies.
The BER is the capped base cost of running the scheme and excludes statutory and regulatory levies such as STT, GST, stamp duty, SEBI fees and exchange fees.
Statutory and regulatory levies on trades are charged at actuals, over and above the permitted brokerage limits.
SEBI also tightened the brokerage that a scheme may pay.
Part of the apparent fall in limits comes from statutory levies being moved outside the base figure, not from those costs disappearing.
Expense limits differ by scheme category and by the size of the scheme.
Schemes may choose a base expense ratio that varies with performance, subject to conditions set by SEBI.
Direct and regular plans of the same scheme have different expense ratios, and the direct plan is lower because it carries no distributor commission.
SEBI requires expenses to be disclosed separately for direct and regular plans.
Fund houses publish the current expense ratio of each scheme on their websites, so check the current figure there.
The expense ratio is one of several things to read in the scheme documents, along with the investment objective and the risk level.

title: SIP vs Lump Sum Investing: How the Two Methods Differ
topic: SIP versus lump sum investing: how the methods differ
outline: Costs, exit load and holding periods
facts: This article compares two ways of investing in a mutual fund scheme: a lump sum and a SIP.
A lump sum investment puts the whole amount into a scheme on one date. A SIP puts in a fixed amount at regular intervals, such as monthly.
Both methods are used to invest in the same mutual fund schemes. A SIP is a method of investing, not a separate product.
A lump sum buys all its units at the NAV of a single date. A SIP buys units at the NAV of each instalment date, so the average purchase cost depends on prices across those dates.
When the NAV is low a SIP instalment buys more units, and when it is high it buys fewer. This is called rupee cost averaging.
Rupee cost averaging reduces dependence on a single entry date, but it does not protect against losses.
A lump sum needs the full amount to be available at once. A SIP lets an investor commit smaller amounts out of regular income.
A SIP is set up through an auto-debit instruction (mandate) with the investor's bank and continues until it is stopped or the stated number of instalments is complete.
Minimum amounts and available frequencies differ by fund house and scheme, so check the scheme documents.

Each SIP instalment is treated as a separate purchase, so exit load periods and holding periods for tax are counted from the date of each instalment. Check the scheme documents and the current tax rules.
For example, ₹12,000 can be invested as one payment of ₹12,000 or as 12 instalments of ₹1,000. The total is the same, but the purchase dates and NAVs differ.
Neither method guarantees returns, and the NAV can fall as well as rise.
Which method fits depends on when the money is available and how long it will stay invested, and this differs for each investor.

title: What Is an Exit Load in Mutual Funds and When Does It Apply?
topic: What is an exit load in mutual funds and when does it apply
outline: How to check the exit load of a scheme
facts: An exit load is a charge deducted when units are redeemed within a specified period after purchase.
The exit load is expressed as a percentage of the redemption amount.
For example, redeeming units worth ₹1,00,000 within the exit load period, with an exit load of 1%, leads to a charge of ₹1,000.
Not every scheme has an exit load, and the rate and the period differ by scheme. A scheme with no exit load is not necessarily better, and one with an exit load is not necessarily worse.
Exit load details are disclosed in the scheme documents, in the section on fees and expenses.
An exit load applies only if units are redeemed within the stated period. After that period no exit load is charged.
The exit load collected from investors is credited back to the scheme and not kept by the fund house, which benefits the remaining unitholders.
Exit loads discourage investors from leaving too soon, because withdrawals can make a fund manager's job harder.
A switch from one scheme to another is treated as a redemption from the source scheme and a purchase in the target scheme, so the exit load of the source scheme can apply.
For a SIP, each instalment has its own exit load period, counted from its own purchase date.
SEBI banned entry loads, so there is no charge for buying units, although other costs such as the expense ratio apply.
The exit load is separate from the expense ratio, which is charged yearly through the NAV.
Liquid and overnight schemes can have a graded exit load for redemptions within a very short period.
A scheme can change its exit load through an addendum, so check the current exit load in the scheme documents or the factsheet before redeeming.

title: KYC for Mutual Funds: What It Is and How the Process Works
topic: KYC for mutual funds: what it is and how the process works
facts: KYC stands for Know Your Customer. SEBI requires KYC to be completed before an investor can invest in mutual funds.
KYC establishes the investor's proof of identity and proof of address.
KYC records are kept by KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) registered with SEBI.
KYC is a one-time exercise. Once it is registered through one SEBI-registered intermediary, the investor generally does not have to repeat it with another fund house or intermediary.
The fund house, a broker or a distributor submits the investor's details to a KRA.
The PAN is central to KYC, and the KYC status can be checked on a KRA or fund house website using the PAN.
KYC can be done online, for example with Aadhaar-based verification using an OTP sent to the mobile number linked to Aadhaar, or offline by submitting a KYC form with documents.
Only specified officially valid documents are accepted as proof of identity and address, and SEBI has changed the list over time, so check the current list with the KRA or fund house.
A KYC status of Validated means the KRA has verified the identity document and the PAN-Aadhaar link, so the investor can invest across fund houses without submitting documents again.
A status of Registered can mean the investor has to complete extra steps with a new intermediary.
Details such as address, mobile number and email can be updated through the KRA or the fund house when they change.
Standard investor-education notices say to invest only through SEBI-registered mutual funds.

title: How to Read a Mutual Fund Factsheet: Section by Section
topic: How to read a mutual fund factsheet section by section
facts: A factsheet is a short monthly document published by a fund house that summarises a scheme.
SEBI requires fund houses to publish factsheets every month.
Factsheets are available on fund house websites and on AMFI's website.
A factsheet typically shows the scheme's category and investment objective, its NAV, its assets under management and details of the fund manager.
The portfolio section shows the largest holdings and the split across asset types and sectors.
Past performance is shown over different periods and compared with the scheme's benchmark index. Past performance does not guarantee future results.
The benchmark is the index against which the scheme's returns are compared, and it should suit the category of the scheme.
The expense ratio is shown as a yearly percentage of assets, and the exit load is listed.
The portfolio turnover ratio shows how actively the fund trades, and frequent trading adds costs inside the fund.

Risk measures such as standard deviation, beta and the Sharpe ratio may be shown. Beta shows how much a scheme moves relative to its benchmark, and the Sharpe ratio measures return above a risk-free rate relative to risk.
The riskometer is a SEBI-mandated colour-coded indicator of a scheme's risk, with six levels from Low to Very High.
A change of fund manager can change how a scheme is run, so the factsheet lists the manager and how long they have managed the scheme.
A factsheet shows the latest month, so an older factsheet will not show recent changes.
The factsheet is a summary. The scheme information document has the full terms.

title: Open-Ended, Close-Ended and Interval Funds: How They Differ
topic: Open-ended, close-ended and interval mutual fund schemes: how they differ
facts: Mutual fund schemes can be classified by structure into three types: open-ended, close-ended and interval.
An open-ended scheme is available for purchase and redemption on an ongoing basis and has no fixed maturity period. Its key feature is liquidity.
Open-ended schemes do not have to be listed on a stock exchange, and investors transact with the fund house at prices related to the NAV.
Because an open-ended scheme accepts purchases at any time, it allows regular investments such as a SIP.
A close-ended scheme has a stipulated maturity period, and units are offered during the new fund offer period.
SEBI regulations require close-ended schemes to be listed on a stock exchange so that investors have an exit route. After the offer, investors buy or sell units on the exchange.
The price of listed units on the exchange can differ from the NAV.
Some close-ended schemes also let investors sell units back to the fund house through periodic repurchase.
An interval scheme combines features of open-ended and close-ended schemes. It is open for purchase or redemption only during pre-specified intervals.
Units of an interval scheme must also be listed on a stock exchange.
Fixed maturity plans are close-ended schemes with a fixed tenure that matches the maturity of their investments.
SEBI has revised its scheme categorisation framework, so check the current categories in the scheme documents.
Before investing, check the scheme documents for when units can be bought or redeemed and for any exit load.

title: What Is a Credit Score in India and What Goes Into It?
topic: What is a credit score in India and what goes into it
outline: What is not in the score
How to check your score and report
Why errors and late payments matter
facts: A credit score is a three-digit number that summarises a person's credit history. In India it generally ranges from 300 to 900.
The CIBIL score is provided by TransUnion CIBIL. India has four credit bureaus: TransUnion CIBIL, Equifax, Experian and CRIF High Mark.
Credit bureaus are regulated by the RBI under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005.
The score is calculated from information that lenders report to the bureau about loans and credit cards.
CIBIL says its score is calculated mainly from payment history, credit utilisation, age of credit and enquiries.
Payment history shows whether EMIs and credit card bills were paid on time and in full, and it is generally treated as the most important factor.
Credit utilisation is how much of the available credit limit is being used.
A credit enquiry is recorded when a lender checks a credit report in connection with a loan or card application.
Income and employment details may appear in a credit report, but the score is calculated from credit account and enquiry information, not from salary or employer.
A higher score generally signals lower risk to lenders, but each lender sets its own criteria and no score guarantees approval.
RBI guidelines entitle a person to one free full credit report, including the score, every calendar year from each credit bureau.
Checking your own report is treated as a soft enquiry and does not lower the score.
Lenders now report data to the bureaus more frequently than before under RBI directions, so recent payments appear in reports sooner.
Errors in a credit report can lower a score, and they can be raised with the credit bureau.
A missed payment can stay visible on a credit report for a period of time.
